source.title: Training Dynamics Underlying Language Model Scaling Laws: Loss Deceleration and Zero-Sum Learning
source.authors: Andrei Mircea; Supriyo Chakraborty; Nima Chitsazan; M. Naphade; Sambit Sahu; Irina Rish; Ekaterina Lobacheva

record.tranche_reason: The study measures how language-model loss changes with model size and training progress, and refines a simple power-law account by reporting piecewise-linear loss curves, loss deceleration, and setup-dependent results.
record.gate_note: The study's main scaling-loss measurements and downstream comparisons are included. Its zero-sum-learning analyses explain the proposed mechanism but do not directly measure a claim version. Results used only to characterize gradients or sharpness, and the batch-size/sequence-length ablation results, are not included as rows.
record.test_reason: The study measures loss scaling and broken power-law training trajectories, tests schedule and optimizer dependence, and compares downstream performance at matched pretraining loss. Its strongest evidence concerns V7; V1 receives preliminary parameter-scaling evidence and V6 receives a conditional qualification.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is substantially correct. The authors identify early loss deceleration and argue that larger models generally lower its loss level and improve the subsequent loss-improvement rate. They attribute deceleration primarily to zero-sum learning through opposing per-example gradients, and suggest targeting it to improve models independently of scale. They treat the proposed parameter-scaling functional form as preliminary. Strict monotonicity is not borne out by every Table 1 entry, and learning-rate decay introduces an additional scale-dependent improvement outside the principal explanation.
record.recipe_differences: The study adapts the Kaplan et al. training setup and measures language-model loss across sizes, but uses OLMo-derived models and data, a trapezoidal schedule without cooldown in its main runs, and one-break BNSL fits to characterize training dynamics. It does not reproduce a compute-optimal allocation sweep.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported loss-deceleration measurements vary with learning-rate schedule and optimizer. Batch size and sequence length also affect some loss measurements, although the corresponding ablation rows were omitted under the 60-row limit.

fits_no_version.finding: The fitted post-deceleration exponent rd appears to follow a power law with model size.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The post-deceleration training-progress exponent itself scales approximately as a power of parameter count.

record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: The parameter-scaling trends in Appendix B.6 are explicitly preliminary and based on limited datapoints. The principal runs cover 14M–472M parameters, with OLMo-1B and OLMo-7B taken from prior work and differing training details. The paper notes that logged batch losses are noisy measurements of validation loss and that some OLMo results rely on training curves. Downstream task values are shown only in figures, without tabulated uncertainty.
record.rows_left_out: The 60-row limit was reached. Omitted: batch-size and sequence-length deceleration results (Appendix C.1, Table 5 and Figures 23–25); early-step loss-improvement comparisons (Table 2); and additional zero-sum-learning and gradient analyses (Sections 3 and Appendices B.1–B.5). The batch-size/sequence-length results report that larger batches improve Ld, longer sequences improve rd on training curves but do not transfer to fixed validation batches, and neither setting discernibly changes measured ZSL.

untested.parts: Controlled held-out-loss scaling over several orders of magnitude with other resources demonstrably non-bottlenecking; independent parameter, token and compute laws. The exploratory Ld fit uses losses at different transition steps, and the main fitted curves use online training-batch losses as validation proxies.
No small-run fit is prospectively evaluated on runs orders of magnitude larger. The within-trajectory final-loss approximation is not such an extrapolation test.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep or compute-optimal parameter/token exponents.
No controlled depth/width or architecture comparison at fixed parameter count; the NanoGPT comparison changes several aspects of setup.
No other modality, repeated-data regime, fine-tuning or transfer scaling test.
No quantitative downstream scaling-law fit, out-of-sample forecast or broad predictability evaluation. The result concerns two OLMo sizes, training phases and four tasks.
No compute-optimal split, parameter-counting comparison, controlled comparison of fitting procedures, or direct explanation of disagreement between published laws.

missing.what: The pre-break slopes, changes in slope and fit errors directly establish the bend underlying the V7 verdict: c0 is 0.17–0.28, c1 is negative for every model, and RSLE is 0.008–0.015. Existing rows contain only post-break rates and breakpoint losses.

Deceleration steps td are absent despite being central to the schedule and optimizer comparisons. Main small-model td values are 4600–6000; cosine-decay values are 3653–5198. AdamW, Muon and AdEMAMix give 5650, 1569 and 5673 respectively.

Cosine decay improves final loss increasingly with size in the controlled small-model sweep: 0.02 at 14M versus 0.11 at 472M. The authors explicitly describe this as a complementary scale-dependent mechanism outside their principal explanation; the scalar rows record the values but omit this cross-size result.

record.verdict_notes: Remove the record's V7 limits_scope verdict: untested compute-optimal allocation and fitting-method comparisons belong under untested. Do not infer a V1 failure from deceleration without establishing the version's non-bottleneck conditions; a fixed model can become capacity-limited as training continues. Likewise, decreasing final loss alone does not establish a power law. The declared batch-size, sequence-length and early-step omissions are not repeated as missing. All judgments use the supplied text; task-specific figure coordinates were unavailable.

versions.untested_parts: The study varies model size and reports loss-related scaling results, but does not test independent scaling with training-token count or compute while holding the other factors non-bottlenecking. The exploratory parameter-scaling fits are explicitly described as limited.
No test of whether laws fitted on small runs predict the loss of much larger runs.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep or estimate of compute-optimal parameter and token counts.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
The study is limited to transformer language-model training on web-scale text; it does not test other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer as scaling regimes.
The downstream comparison covers OLMo-1B and OLMo-7B checkpoints on four tasks; it does not test broad downstream predictability across models, scales, or tasks.

The study varies training setups and observes bends in training-loss curves, but does not test compute-optimal allocation, parameter-counting choices, alternative fitting methods against one another, or why published scaling laws disagree.

rows.subject: 14M–472M model-size sweep
rows.operation_detail: Explore fitted trends in the deceleration parameters across model sizes.
rows.measure: power-law trend in Ld with model size
rows.value: Figure only; the authors say Ld seems to exhibit power-law scaling.
rows.note: The authors call this preliminary, based on limited datapoints, and not a key result.
rows.check: The authors report an apparent power-law trend, so preliminary evidence should not automatically be coded partial.
